## Proof

We determine the Lebesgue measure (2-dimensional) of
$$E = \{(a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^2 \mid a-b\in\mathbb{Q}\}.$$

**Step 1: Decompose $E$ as a countable union of lines.**

For each $q\in\mathbb{Q}$, define the line
$$L_q = \{(a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^2 \mid a - b = q\}.$$
Equivalently, $L_q = \{(t+q, t) : t\in\mathbb{R}\}$, which is the line of slope $1$ in the $(a,b)$-plane passing through $(q,0)$.

Since $a-b\in\mathbb{Q}$ holds exactly when $a-b=q$ for some $q\in\mathbb{Q}$, we have
$$E = \bigcup_{q\in\mathbb{Q}} L_q.$$

**Step 2: Each $L_q$ has 2-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero.**

The line $L_q$ is an affine 1-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2$. Concretely, it is the graph of the affine function $b \mapsto b+q$, i.e. $a = b+q$. A standard result in measure theory states that the graph of any measurable function $\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ has 2-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. 

For completeness, we verify this directly. For any $n\in\mathbb{N}$, the segment of $L_q$ with $b\in[-n,n]$ lies in the rectangle $[q-n, q+n]\times[-n,n]$, which has area $4n^2$. Partition $[-n,n]$ into $N$ subintervals of width $2n/N$; over each, the line sweeps a strip of width $2n/N$ and height $2n$, of area $(2n/N)\cdot 2n = 4n^2/N$. Summing over all $N$ strips gives $4n^2$, but more sharply, covering the line segment by $N$ squares of side $2n/N$ gives total area $N\cdot(2n/N)^2 = 4n^2/N\to 0$ as $N\to\infty$. Hence the segment of $L_q$ in $[-n,n]^2$ has measure zero. Taking the countable union over $n$ shows $\lambda_2(L_q)=0$.

**Step 3: Countable subadditivity gives $\lambda_2(E)=0$.**

Since $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable, $E$ is a countable union of measure-zero sets. By countable subadditivity of the Lebesgue measure,
$$\lambda_2(E) = \lambda_2\!\left(\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb{Q}} L_q\right) \le \sum_{q\in\mathbb{Q}} \lambda_2(L_q) = \sum_{q\in\mathbb{Q}} 0 = 0.$$

Since measure is nonnegative, $\lambda_2(E)=0$.

**Conclusion.** The set $E$ is a countable union of parallel lines (one for each rational number), each of 2-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. Therefore
$$\lambda_2(E) = 0.$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
